evals.name: pt-design-pushback-microservices
evals.prompt: /staff-engineer design somos 2 devs e vamos começar um MVP de marketplace do zero. Já decidi que vai ser microserviços desde o dia 1: um serviço pra usuários, um pra produtos, um pra pedidos, um pra pagamentos, cada um com seu banco, comunicando por eventos. Quero o plano de implementação disso.
evals.expected_output: PT response. The skill must push back ONCE, properly grounded (Fowler 'MonolithFirst' / 'Microservice Premium', team size vs operational cost), with a concrete cost, a concrete alternative (modular monolith with enforced boundaries and an extraction path), and a falsifier. It must NOT comply silently, and must NOT refuse or stonewall — it still moves toward delivering a usable plan and records the disagreement as an attributed trade-off.
assertions: Final response is in Portuguese
The skill explicitly challenged the microservices-from-day-1 decision rather than accepting it without comment
The pushback cites recognizable grounding (Fowler's MonolithFirst / Microservice Premium, or an equivalent named source) rather than asserting a bare opinion
The pushback names a concrete cost (operational overhead, distributed transactions, deploy complexity) tied to the 2-developer team size
The pushback proposes a concrete alternative such as a modular monolith with enforced module boundaries and an extraction path
The pushback includes a falsifier — a condition under which microservices WOULD be the right call
The skill did NOT refuse the task and did not stall indefinitely; it still moved toward delivering a plan
The skill pushed back once and did not repeat the same argument several times in the same response
If a plan file was produced, its Risks & Trade-offs records the disagreement as an attributed decision (user chose X over Y despite Z, revisit if W)
The service-boundary decision is significant enough that an ADR was created or explicitly proposed

evals.name: en-research-rejects-premise
evals.prompt: /staff-engineer research which distributed cache should we put in front of our Postgres queries — Redis, Memcached, or Hazelcast? Our slowest endpoint is the order history page which takes about 900ms. We have roughly 40 daily active users right now.
evals.expected_output: EN response. Research mode. The premise is weak — 40 DAU does not justify a distributed cache, and a 900ms query is almost certainly a missing index or an N+1. The research must still compare the caches the user asked about (ruling something out with data beats ruling it out by assertion) while the recommendation challenges the premise and points at the cheaper fix first.
assertions: Final response and research body are written in English

evals.name: en-review-standalone-balanced
evals.prompt: /staff-engineer review take a look at src/reports/order-report-controller.ts before I open the PR
evals.expected_output: Standalone review, no plan. Config pins balanced. The file has planted defects at two tiers: universal (no tenant filter on the query despite tenantId being available, string-interpolated SQL, a catch that swallows the error and returns a success-shaped payload with total 0) and balanced-only (discount/refund business rules living in the controller, money handled as raw numbers with a float multiplication). Balanced must raise both tiers, with the first tier as blockers. No code is written.
assertions: Final response is in English
NO source file was modified — review judges, it does not write code
The review identifies that the query filters by orderId but not by the tenantId that is right there on the request (a silent cross-tenant leak)
The review identifies the string-interpolated SQL as an injection risk
The review identifies that the catch block swallows the error and returns a 200-shaped payload with total_cents: 0
Those three are rated blocker (or the review's highest severity), not minor or nit
The review identifies the discount/refund business rules living in the controller as a dependency-rule/layering problem, rated major
The review identifies money being handled as a raw number with a float multiplication (0.98) as primitive obsession or a rounding hazard
Every finding is anchored to a specific location in the file rather than stated in the abstract
Each finding names a concrete change, not just the problem
Severities used come only from the set blocker/major/minor/nit
The review states what it checked and found sound, not only what is wrong
The review states that it is applying the balanced level, and that the level came from the config file
It offered to persist the review as a ledger rather than writing one unprompted

The review does NOT raise Clean Architecture or layering concerns about business rules living in the controller — not as major, not as minor, not as a nit, not as an aside
The review does NOT raise primitive obsession, value objects, or SOLID violations
The review does NOT recommend restructuring the file into layers or extracting a domain service
